1.pericope_label: And when any will offer a meat offering unto the Lord, his offering shall be of fine flour; and he shall pour oil upon it, and put frankincense thereon: And he shall bring it to Aaron's sons the priests: and he shall take thereout his handful of the flour thereof, and of the oil thereof, with all the frankincense thereof; and the priest shall burn the memorial of it upon the altar, to be an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the Lord: And the remnant of the meat offering shall be Aaron's and his sons': it is a thing most holy of the offerings of the Lord made by fire.

schools.summary: Render the opening words as an oblation of a meat offering, since the same two words are so rendered later in the chapter, and set out the enumeration before expounding: the meat offerings occupy the whole chapter and fall into three kinds, of which this is the first, fine flour with oil and frankincense. Identify the flour precisely. It was of wheat, worth double the ordinary barley flour, and because of its constant use in the sacrifices it was kept among the Temple stores. Explain the oil by the diet rather than by symbol, oil standing to the food of Israel as butter does to ours, so that the offerer is told to put some into the preparation to make it more palatable to the priests who were to eat part of it; and explain the frankincense by the altar, as designed to counteract the smell of the quantity of flesh burnt there, which is why the following verse directs that all of it be burnt. Correct the English of the second verse as well: better, the priest shall take from it a handful of its flour and of its oil with all its frankincense, and burn this as its memorial. Give the reason for the name, that it was designed to bring the worshipper into the grateful remembrance of God and to remind him of the promise to accept the service rendered according to command, and cite the psalm asking that the Lord remember all thine offerings, and the word to Cornelius that his prayers and his alms were come up for a memorial. On the remnant, note that with the exception of the handful and of all the frankincense the offering belonged to the priests, who divided it among them and consumed it in the court alone. Then classify. The offerings were of two grades, less holy and most holy: the former, such as the thank offerings and the firstlings, might be eaten in any clean place within the holy city and by the priests' families, while the latter, which include the meat offerings here described, could be eaten only in the court of the sanctuary and by the priests themselves.

Begin with the noun used for the offerer, which is soul rather than man, the Targum rendering it a man from his nobler part; and take the Jewish comment that the word suits a freewill offering made with the whole heart and soul, as though the offerer presented his own soul to the Lord. Distinguish accordingly between the meat offerings fixed and required at set times, the daily sacrifice, the consecration of priests, the waving of the sheaf, and this one, which is why the law reads when any man will offer. Canvass the derivations of the name without settling on one: from a root meaning to bring or offer, in which case it is a name common to offerings of any sort; from a root meaning to delight, the offering being of a sweet savour; or from a root not now in use which in the Chaldee gives a gift or present. Then state the rule the chapter is teaching. Nothing but what is pure is to be offered, which is why fine flour is required and the bran excluded, while the oil improves the savour and the frankincense imparts a fragrant odour. God is attracted neither by sweetness of taste nor by pleasant scents, but it was useful to teach a rude people by such symbols, lest they corrupt his service by their own foolish inventions. Insist on the mediation. Whatever is consecrated to God must be delivered into the priest's hand, private persons being shut out from that honour, so that Christ's peculiar dignity might remain to him, that access should be sought through him alone, and that all men might know no worship pleases God except what he sanctifies; the substance of the type appears where the Apostle says that by him we offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually. On the remnant, observe that God provides for the maintenance of his priests, from which an argument is drawn for the support of the ministers of the Gospel, and that those made priests unto God by Christ have a right to feed by faith upon him who is himself both the altar and the meat offering.

Correct the title first. It is a meal offering, not a meat offering, the familiar word being an ancient false print which has run through many editions of the English bible. Then count the kinds, taking the five that Calmet distinguishes: simple flour or meal; cakes and wafers, or whatever was baked in the oven; cakes baked in the pan; cakes baked on the frying-pan or gridiron; and green ears of corn parched. Set the offering historically. This was very likely the earliest oblation offered to the Supreme Being, probably in use before sin entered into the world and therefore before bloody sacrifices had been ordained; the offering of green ears dried by the fire was properly the gratitude offering for a good seed time and the prospect of a plentiful harvest, and appears to have been the offering brought by Cain. Note that no animal is included here, that the offering was not used by way of atonement or expiation but merely in a eucharistic way, expressing gratitude for the produce of the soil, and that the flour of any grain used for food was in all likelihood equally proper, barley meal being called by the same name elsewhere. Then give the reasons for the appointment: that these are the things of greatest necessity and benefit to man, so that it is meet God should be served with them and owned and praised as the giver of them; that it condescends to the poor, so that they might not want an offering for God, and shows that God would accept even the meanest services when offered with a sincere mind; and that these were the provisions for the feast presented to God and for the use of the priests. Read the ingredients as figures. The oil may note the graces of the Holy Ghost, which scripture compares to oil and to anointing, and which are necessary to make any offering acceptable; the frankincense plainly designs Christ's satisfaction and intercession, which is compared to a sweet odour. On the handful, say it was burnt to put God in mind of his covenant with their fathers, or the offerer in mind that all he has of that kind is God's; note with Ainsworth that neither oil nor incense was offered with the sin and jealousy offerings, since those were not offerings of memorial but brought iniquities to remembrance; and add that all the frankincense was burnt, because from it the priest could derive no advantage.

Mark first which offerings the chapter governs. Some meat offerings were only appendices to the burnt offerings, offered with the daily sacrifice and with the peace offerings and having drink offerings joined to them, and in those the quantity was appointed; this law concerns the meat offerings that were offered by themselves, whenever a man saw cause thus to express his devotion, and the first offering we read of in scripture was of that kind. Give two reasons for the appointment. It was a condescension to the poor and their ability, so that those who themselves lived only upon bread and cakes might offer to God out of their own coarse and homely fare, and by making a little cake first for God's altar, as the widow of Sarepta did for his prophet, might procure such a blessing upon the handful of meal in the barrel and the oil in the cruse that it should not fail. And it was a proper acknowledgment of the mercy of God to them in their food, like a quitrent by which they testified their dependence upon God, their thankfulness to him and their expectations from him as their owner and bountiful benefactor; so those who now with a grateful and charitable heart deal out their bread to the hungry offer an acceptable meat offering, and the prophet laments it as one of the direful effects of famine that the meat offering was thereby cut off from the house of the Lord. Then run through the laws of it. The ingredients must always be fine flour and oil, oil being to them in their food what butter is now to us, poured upon the flour if the offering was undressed and mingled with it if cooked. Flour unbaked must have frankincense put upon it besides, for the perfuming of the altar. It was to be presented by the offerer to the priest, which is called bringing it to the Lord, since the priests were God's receivers and were ordained to offer gifts. Part was burnt upon the altar for a memorial, in token of their mindfulness of God's bounty in giving them all things richly to enjoy, and the consuming of it by fire might remind them that they deserved to have all the fruits of the earth thus burnt up, and that it was of the Lord's mercies that they were not. The remainder was given to the priests, a thing most holy, not to be eaten by the offerers as the peace offerings were, so that those who served at the altar should live upon the altar, and live comfortably.

4.pericope_label: And if thou bring an oblation of a meat offering baken in the oven, it shall be unleavened cakes of fine flour mingled with oil, or unleavened wafers anointed with oil. And if thy oblation be a meat offering baken in a pan, it shall be of fine flour unleavened, mingled with oil. Thou shalt part it in pieces, and pour oil thereon: it is a meat offering. And if thy oblation be a meat offering baken in the fryingpan, it shall be made of fine flour with oil.

schools.summary: Take the second class as a group: preparations baked with oil, in the oven, on the pan, or cooked in a pot. Identify the oven from what is still used in the East, probably the portable pot open at the top, about three feet high and liable to be broken; once the vessel is thoroughly heated the dough, made into large thin oval cakes resembling pancakes or Scotch oatcakes, is dexterously thrown against the sides, the aperture above is covered, and the bread is completely baked in a few minutes, soft enough at first to be rolled up like paper but hardening and growing crisp as it is kept. For the second vessel prefer a flat plate to a pan. This is probably the iron fire-plate with a convex surface, placed horizontally upon stones about nine inches from the ground with the fire kindled underneath, used by the Arabs to this day, on which the large thin cakes and the thin wafer bread are laid and baked in comparatively few minutes. Corroborate it from the travellers: such flat plates are still in use among the Turcomans of Syria and the Armenians, while the Berbers and Kabyles of Africa use shallow iron frying-pans for the purpose and call them by the very name, no doubt, that the Greek translators chose here. Fix the place of the operation in the court of the sanctuary, where the vessels of ministration were kept. For the third, refuse the gridiron the Greek version supplies, and argue from the root, which means to boil, that a vessel for boiling must be intended, so that we have to think of cakes boiled in oil; render it boiled in a pan, a deeper vessel answering rather to our stew-pan or pot. On the parting, note that the cake thus baked was not to be offered as a whole but broken up in pieces and mingled with oil, just as the Bedouins break the cakes they bake in the hot ashes into small pieces, bread broken and steeped in oil, butter, milk or sweet juices being still a favourite dish among them.

Work from the words first and then from the travellers. Derive the name of the oven from a root meaning to split or divide, so called because of its burning, dissolving and melting heat; take the second vessel for a flat iron plate placed over the fire, such as is called a griddle in some countries; and suppose the third to be the same with the shallow earthen vessel the Arabs call a ta-jen, used not only to fry in but for other purposes. Add only that the oven was one made in the sanctuary for that use. Then let the eastern evidence be gathered at length, since the variety of methods of preparing the meat offerings which Moses names is not to be understood from a single report. Note that in the cities and villages of Barbary there are public ovens, but that among the Bedouins who live in tents and the Kabyles who live in miserable hovels in the mountains the bread, made into thin cakes, is baked either immediately upon the coals or else in such a vessel, and that the word the Greek version uses for the pan is the same in sound as well as in meaning as the name that vessel still bears among them. Grant that the account is curious but that it does not give all the eastern ways of baking, and so does not furnish a complete comment on the variety here. Bring in the older travellers, who saw bread baked in the deserts of Arabia on ground heated for the purpose, the cakes covered with ashes and coals and turned several times until they were baked enough, while some of the Arabians kept in their tents stones or copper plates made on purpose for baking; and the later ones, who describe iron hearths used for the same work, and the small convex iron plates most commonly used in Persia and among the wandering people that dwell in tents, as being the easiest way of baking and done with the least expense.

Take the distinction of the vessels as a matter of law rather than of travel. Note first that this is another kind of meat offering, or the same in another form: the former was only fine flour and oil mixed together with frankincense put upon it, while this was made up into cakes and wafers and baked, and by the Jewish tradition a man who says that a meat offering baked in an oven is upon him may not bring one baked otherwise. Then distinguish the two remaining vessels by their construction rather than by their names. The pan has no lip or covering, and therefore the paste baked upon it must be hard and stiff, that it should not run out; the frying-pan is a deep vessel which has a lip or edge round about it, and the paste which is baked in it is thin and flows. Turn next to the parting in pieces, which answered to the dividing of the pieces of the burnt offering and signified the same thing, and report the rule that all meat offerings prepared in a vessel were obliged to be cut to pieces, one cake of an Israelite's offering being doubled into two and two into four and then divided, each piece about the quantity of an olive. Finally read the whole series of operations together: the mixing of the flour and the kneading, the baking and the frying, the cutting in pieces, and the burning of part upon the altar, all signify the dolorous sufferings of Christ when he was sacrificed for us, to be both an atonement for our sins and food for our faith.

8.pericope_label: And thou shalt bring the meat offering that is made of these things unto the Lord: and when it is presented unto the priest, he shall bring it unto the altar. And the priest shall take from the meat offering a memorial thereof, and shall burn it upon the altar: it is an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the Lord. And that which is left of the meat offering shall be Aaron's and his sons': it is a thing most holy of the offerings of the Lord made by fire. No meat offering, which ye shall bring unto the Lord, shall be made with leaven: for ye shall burn no leaven, nor any honey, in any offering of the Lord made by fire. As for the oblation of the firstfruits, ye shall offer them unto the Lord: but they shall not be burnt on the altar for a sweet savour. And every oblation of thy meat offering shalt thou season with salt; neither shalt thou suffer the salt of the covenant of thy God to be lacking from thy meat offering: with all thine offerings thou shalt offer salt.

schools.summary: Say first that the presentation of an offering made of these things, that is, of the different kinds of pastry just described, resembled in the main what was prescribed for the plain flour at the head of the chapter. Then fill in the later usage: whichever of the three cereal preparations was preferred, the offerer presented it to the priest, who took it to the altar; during the second Temple the pieces were put into a ministering vessel, oil and frankincense were then put upon them, the vessel was carried by the offerer to the priest, and the priest carried it to the altar and brought it to the south-west. Treat the verses that follow as general rules appended to the whole class. Explain the ban on honey by its use: as honey was employed in olden times to produce fermentation, it is excluded like fermented dough. Read the next verse as an exception, better rendered that as an oblation of firstfruits ye may offer them, leaven and honey, which are excluded from the meat offerings, being admissible with firstfruits, which is why the two are mentioned together elsewhere. On salt, observe that it is the contrary to leaven and preserves from putrefaction and corruption, and that it was to be an ingredient not only of the bloodless offerings but of all the animal sacrifices as well. Then trace the phrase. From its antiseptic and savoury qualities salt became the symbol of hospitality, friendship, durability and fidelity; to eat bread and salt together is in the East an expression for a league of mutual amity; when the Arabs make a covenant they put salt on the blade of a sword, from which each puts a little into his mouth, which constitutes them blood relations who remain faithful to one another even in danger of life. Conclude that a covenant of salt, an expression which occurs elsewhere in the law and in the chronicles, denotes an indissoluble alliance and an everlasting covenant, and that to be salted with the salt of the palace means to be bound by sacred obligations of fidelity to the king.

Bring the offering to the tabernacle, or rather to the Lord's priest, and let the memorial be the handful, taken as of the fine flour so also of the pieces of that which was baked, whether in the oven, in the pan, or in the fryingpan, while what is left is simply what was not burnt with fire. On the leaven, note that it might be used in the peace offerings and in the wave loaves but not here, and not only in the handful burnt but in the rest that Aaron and his sons ate; report the rule that all meat offerings are kneaded in hot water and kept that they might not be leavened, so that if what is left of them be leavened a negative precept is transgressed. Then make the rule general: God's service is corrupted if any strange invention be mingled with it, which is what Christ meant in warning his disciples of the leaven of the Pharisees, by which he understood the fictions whereby they had corrupted religion; the Passover forbade leaven for another reason, the haste of the departure, and the Apostle extends it further to the leaven of malice and wickedness. Read it also of Christ, as free from hypocrisy and from all false doctrines, and of his people, that they should be clear of malice and of communion with the profane. On the honey, own that the ground is obscure and survey the guesses of others, that it means sweet fruits such as figs and dates, that the bee is an impure animal, that honey burns with an offensive smell, that it was constantly offered in the Gentile sacrifices; then advance what seems more probable, that cooked honey immediately becomes sour and causes the bread with which it is mixed to ferment, so that the two prohibitions belong together. Allow the firstfruits of honey to be acceptable provided they did not corrupt the offerings of the altar, and cite the Targum, that the leavened bread of the firstfruits was offered, and dates in the time of the firstfruits. On the salt, hold that God's service must not be without savour, and that the true seasoning which gives grace to sacrifices is found nowhere except in his word, so that all modes of worship fabricated by men are rejected as unsavoury; take from the saying that every one shall be salted with fire the exhortation that believers who desire to please God must patiently endure to be refined; and distinguish the salt of the covenant, which is the salt employed according to the inviolable compact of God, from the covenant of salt. Add the figure, that salt speaks of the savouriness and acceptableness of Christ as a meat offering both to his people and to the Father, of the perpetuity of his sacrifice, and of the gracious conversation of those who by faith feed upon him.

Have the offerer himself bring the sacrifice to the priest, and the priest present it before the Lord. On the leaven, refer back to the reason given at the exodus, that they were forced through haste to bring away their meal or dough unleavened, and add that the prohibition binds what is offered of free will, leaven being permitted in other offerings; then take it as forbidden because it produces fermentation and was therefore considered a species of corruption, used to signify hypocrisy and malice, which corrupt the soul, and as signifying what Christ would be and what his people should be, pure and free from all error in the faith and worship of God. On the honey, offer the physical reason first, that it is apt to produce acidity when wrought up with flour paste, or rather apt to gripe and prove purgative, so much so that the College of Physicians have totally left it out of all medicinal preparations, which mattered here because a principal part of these offerings was eaten by the priests as part of their ordinary diet and the offerings of the poorer sort were in greater abundance than most. Then add the other grounds: that it has the same effect as leaven in making dough sour and swelling; that the prohibition stands in opposition to the sacrifices of the Gentiles, in which the use of honey was most frequent; and that it teaches that God's worship is not to be governed by men's fancies and appetites but by God's will. Allow that honey might have a moral reference also, and that Jerome thought it signified carnal pleasures and sensual gratifications, and note the suggestion that the honey meant was a saccharine matter extracted from dates. Grant that both might be offered with the firstfruits, but not burnt on the altar, being reserved for the priests. On the salt, set it opposite the leaven: it preserved from putrefaction and corruption and signified the purity and persevering fidelity necessary in the worship of God, and it is called the salt of the covenant because, as salt is incorruptible, so was the covenant made with the patriarchs relative to the redemption of the world. Add that it signifies incorruption of mind and sincerity of grace, and testifies the communion the worshippers had with God, salt being the great symbol of friendship in all nations and representing the perpetuity of the covenant, so that the neglect of salt in their sacrifices was itself a breach of covenant. Finally show that the heathen thought so too, no sacrifice being performed among them without the salted meal, and give Pliny's chapter at length, down to his remark that human life cannot be lived without it, that the delights of life and the highest mental serenity are named from it, and that the soldier's pay is called a salary from the same word.

Give the leaven its historical reason, in remembrance of the unleavened bread they ate when they came out of Egypt, so much despatch being required in these offerings that it was not convenient they should stay for the leavening of them. Then improve the New Testament comparison two ways: pride and hypocrisy are likened to leaven because they swell like leaven, and malice and wickedness because they sour like leaven, so that we are to take heed of the sins which will certainly spoil the acceptableness of our spiritual sacrifices, lifting up pure hands without wrath and keeping our gospel feasts with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. Give the honey its reason too, that though Canaan flowed with it, to eat much honey is not good, since it turns to choler and bitterness in the stomach though it be luscious to the taste; and mention the opinion that the chief reason for both prohibitions was that the Gentiles used them much in their sacrifices, God's people being forbidden to learn the way of the heathen, his services being the reverse of their idolatrous ones. Add the allegorical application some make, that leaven signifies grief and sadness of spirit and honey sensual pleasure and mirth, both of which are to be avoided in the service of God and a mean observed between the extremes, since the sorrow of the world worketh death and love to the delights of sense is a great enemy to holy love. Then turn to the salt. The altar was the table of the Lord, and salt being always set upon our tables, God would have it always used at his; it is called the salt of the covenant because, as men confirmed their covenants with each other by eating and drinking together, at all which collations salt was used, so God by accepting his people's gifts and feasting them upon his sacrifices confirmed his covenant with them, and among the ancients salt was a symbol of friendship. Add the practical detail that the salt for the sacrifice was not brought by the offerers but provided at the public charge, as the wood was, and that there was a chamber in the court of the temple called the chamber of salt where they laid it up. Then ask whether that which is unsavoury can be eaten without salt, and answer that God would hereby intimate that their sacrifices in themselves were unsavoury; the saints, who are living sacrifices, must have salt in themselves, their speech must be always with grace, and all our religious performances must be seasoned with it, for Christianity is the salt of the earth.

No: it might be used in the peace offerings and in the wave loaves, but not in the meat offering
No: the prohibition binds the freewill offering, leaven being permitted in others

14.pericope_label: And if thou offer a meat offering of thy firstfruits unto the Lord, thou shalt offer for the meat offering of thy firstfruits green ears of corn dried by the fire, even corn beaten out of full ears. And thou shalt put oil upon it, and lay frankincense thereon: it is a meat offering. And the priest shall burn the memorial of it, part of the beaten corn thereof, and part of the oil thereof, with all the frankincense thereof: it is an offering made by fire unto the Lord.

schools.summary: Name the third kind plainly: the meat offering of firstfruits, that is, of the first ripening corn. Then raise the question of arrangement before the question of substance. These verses should properly come immediately after the permission granted for leaven and honey with the firstfruits, since the verse about salt concludes the directions about the different kinds of bloodless offerings with general remarks applying to all the sacrifices; transpositions of this sort are not uncommon in the Hebrew scriptures, and the reader should be told so rather than left to force a connection. Then parse the two descriptive phrases. The first requires the offering in the form of ears parched or roasted by the fire, in other words made from ears which had been roasted at the fire. To this is added a further definition, rubbed out of field-fruit: the noun comes from a root meaning to rub to pieces, and means that which is rubbed to pieces, a word which occurs nowhere in the law except in these verses; while the word rendered field-fruit is applied generally to a corn-field, and in the prophets to cultivated ground as distinguished from desert, and is used here by metonymy for what the ground bears. Justify the offering from ordinary life. Parched or roasted corn was, and still is, a favourite article of food in the East, as the histories show again and again, in the law of the wave sheaf, at the keeping of the passover in the plains of Jericho, in the provisions carried to the camp, in what was set before the fugitive king, and in the parched corn handed to the gleaner at the meal; it was therefore an appropriate meat offering, and the regulations laid down for it are accordingly the same as those given for the other two kinds.

Settle first whether the offering was owed or volunteered, and report the Jewish authorities on both sides. One takes it that this was not any of the offerings of firstfruits which they were obliged to bring, as at the passover, at pentecost, or at the feast of tabernacles, but a freewill offering; others understand it of the meat offering of the Omer, which was offered up on the sixteenth of Nisan, and this is the general sense of the Jewish writers. Then distinguish it from the firstfruits proper on the same ground: those were paid in obedience to the enactment of the law, while this was voluntary, so that if any one chose to add anything to the firstfruits of his new corn, the rule is laid down for him. Take the two descriptions of the grain as one thing rather than two, the ears being dried in the fire so that they might be the more easily pounded and so burnt mixed with oil and frankincense. Then press the word full. Full ears are required so that the people may select them and not offer anything poor or stunted, which is the same rule of purity that governed the fine flour at the beginning of the chapter. On the handling, note that the oil and the frankincense were put either upon the ears of corn dried, or upon the fine flour of them when ground, in like manner as they were put upon the fine flour of wheat and upon the cakes and wafers baked; and that the memorial burnt was that which was taken out of the offering for a memorial, the same with the handful, being part of the beaten corn, or of that which was ground in a mill, and part of the oil, with all the frankincense, an offering made by fire unto the Lord.

Begin with the fact that this is real food. Green, or half-ripe, ears of wheat parched with fire is a species of food in use among the poor people of Palestine and Egypt to the present day, so that what is commanded here is nothing exotic. Draw the picture that follows from it. Because the tabernacle was God's house, where he had the golden table and the shewbread, he is represented as keeping a table among his people, and so represents himself as partaking with them of all the aliments that were in use, and even as sitting down with the poor to a repast on parched corn. Then say what the offering meant: these green ears were presented as a sort of eucharistical offering for the blessings of seed time and for the prospect of a plentiful harvest. Insist that it was voluntary, of a man's own free will, since there were other firstfruits, and of several sorts, which were prescribed, and whose time, quality and proportion were appointed by God. Then close the chapter by reflecting on the command to offer salt with every oblation, which the Jews punctually observed. Salt has two grand properties: it seasons and renders palatable the principal aliments used for the support of life, and it prevents putrefaction and decay. The covenant of God, that is, his agreement with his people, is called a covenant of salt to denote its stable and undecaying nature, and to point out its importance and utility in the preservation of the life of the soul; and the grace of God by Christ Jesus is represented under the same emblem because of its relishing, nourishing and preserving quality. Without it no offering, no sacrifice, no religious service, no work even of charity and mercy, can be acceptable in the sight of God. And read the fire itself as a figure: it denotes the fervency of spirit which ought to be in all our religious services, holy love being the fire by which all our offerings must be made, or else they are not of a sweet savour to God.

debates.question: Was this offering required or voluntary?

sides.position: Voluntary, as against the firstfruits which were paid in obedience to the law
Of a man's own free will, there being other firstfruits whose time and proportion God appointed
The Jewish writers divide: one takes it for a freewill offering, others for the offering of the Omer brought on the sixteenth of Nisan

outliers.note: Alone argues that these verses stand out of place and should follow immediately on the permission for leaven and honey, the verse about salt being a general conclusion to the whole class of bloodless offerings.
Alone draws from the tabernacle the picture of God keeping a table among his people, partaking of the same food they live on and sitting down with the poor to a repast of parched corn.
